beats.script_body: In 1891 the Metropolitan Club was established under the chairmanship of banker J. P. Morgan. It is a private club, and the building was inspired by the architecture of Italian palazzos. The inside, unfortunately accessible only to members, is extravagantly decorated with Corinthian columns, rich red carpets, marble, and velvet.

beats.script_body: 726 Madison Avenue was built in 1932 for the Bank of Manhattan Company. The building's Georgian-style architecture had not been in fashion for nearly a century, and as a result it seems completely out of place on this posh street.

beats.trigger_address: 47-49 E 65th St, between Madison and Park avenues
beats.script_body: The Roosevelt House is actually two houses with one shared entrance. Sarah Delano Roosevelt gave the house to her son Franklin and his new bride, Eleanor, and the dominating mother lived at number 47. In 1921 and 1922, FDR and his wife lived at number 49 while he was recovering from polio. The house always remained their home base whenever they were in New York. Following Sarah's death in 1941, the house was sold.

name: Park Avenue Armory
short_description: NEW POI flagged. Source address: 643 Park Ave. (at 66th St.).
_poi_role_reasoning: A single named former military building with interior cue; large radius reflects building size but it's narrated as one address you visit, not an area to traverse.
_poi_role_source: a 55,000-square-foot drill hall at its core

beats.script_body: The 7th Regiment Armory, also known as Park Avenue Armory, seems a bit like a fort. The large brick building, dating back to 1880, was once the headquarters of the seventh regiment of the New York National Guard. The interior is beautifully decorated, but after 120 years the building had grown dilapidated. In 2006 the Park Armory Conservancy began significant renovations to transform it into a unique place for unconventional art.

name: West side of Park Avenue, from 68th to 69th streets

beats.poi_name: West side of Park Avenue, from 68th to 69th streets
beats.script_body: The houses on the west side of Park Avenue, from 68th to 69th streets, were saved from demolition in 1965 by Marquesa de Cuevas, a member of the wealthy Rockefeller family. She donated the buildings to her favorite charities, including the Americas Society, the Spanish Institute, and the Istituto Italiano di Cultura. Today you can come here for exhibits, readings, and classes.

short_description: Tier-4: Frick Collection temporary home; 3 Vermeers, Bellini, El Greco, Holbein.

_poi_role_source: Beaux-arts mansion exterior on Fifth Avenue, part of the former Millionaires' Row

beats.script_body: The Frick Collection is located in the former home of the Pittsburgh steel magnate Henry Clay Frick. The collection includes masterpieces from many famous European artists, such as Van Eyck, Bellini, Titian, and Goya. Today the museum maintains the same homey feel as when Frick himself lived here.

name: The Jewish Museum
short_description: Tier-4: 4,000 years of Jewish culture through art; ~800 artifacts.
_poi_role_reasoning: A discrete museum in a French-Gothic mansion, a single stop.
_poi_role_source: French-Gothic mansion exterior of the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue

beats.script_body: The Jewish Museum began in 1904 with 26 objects on display for visitors to view. Today the collection has grown to include 26,000 objects that reflect 4,000 years of Jewish art and culture. You'll find everything from archeological artifacts and paintings to videos and interactive websites.

Visit the museum to see everything from historic to contemporary design, and from one-of-a-kind to mass-produced design objects.

name: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
short_description: Tier-5: Frank Lloyd Wright 1959 spiral landmark; major modern-art collection.
_poi_role_reasoning: A single iconic spiral building you stand before, a discrete stop.
_poi_role_source: Frank Lloyd Wright's windowless spiral facade among the Fifth Avenue towers

beats.script_body: The Guggenheim Museum is one of the most famous buildings by architect Frank Lloyd Wright, and the building's unique architecture is certainly at least as important as the Picassos and Kandinskys hanging inside. For the ultimate experience, take the elevator to the top and then work your way downward. Plan to spend at least half a day in the museum.

She thoroughly valued and appreciated the anonymity afforded her by the people of NYC and often went for walks in Central Park. Jackie lived here until her death in 1994.

name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
short_description: Tier-5: largest museum in the hemisphere, 1.6M sq ft, 3M+ works; flagship NYC attraction.
_poi_role_reasoning: A single flagship museum building you stand before, with interior galleries described as cues.
_poi_role_source: Richard Morris Hunt's limestone edifice, its mountain of steps and redwood-height pillars

beats.script_body: The grand building that houses the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Met, bears a strong resemblance to the Palace of Versailles. In this museum you'll find artwork from ancient times as well as modern art. Various additions have been made to the building over the years, but the 5th Avenue side dates back to 1895-1902. For a nice view, head up to the rooftop garden.

name: Bethesda Terrace
_poi_role_reasoning: A discrete architectural terrace and fountain you stand before, a named feature inside Central Park.
_poi_role_source: Bethesda Terrace is, without a doubt, the architectural heart of the park

beats.script_body: The Bethesda Fountain is the backdrop of many wedding photos; brides and grooms come here nearly every day to pose for pictures, with the lake, rowboats, and the grand buildings of western Manhattan in the background. Bethesda Terrace was one of the first structures in Central Park. The terrace has two levels connected by stately steps. Be sure to walk underneath and admire the gorgeous tiled ceiling.

beats.trigger_address: Central Park, between E 70th and E 71st streets
beats.script_body: The neoclassical Naumburg Bandshell was built in Central Park in 1923. Since then, artists of all ilk have performed here. Famous people such as Martin Luther King Jr. and John Lennon have also stood on this stage. The Mall runs through the middle of the park, from the Bethesda Terrace down to 66th Street, lined with benches where you may have to compete with street artists, roller skaters, and skateboarders for a seat.
